title: Ramanujan Bigraphs and Applications
authors: Shai Evra (The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel), Brooke Feigon (The City College of New York, CUNY Graduate Center, USA), Kathrin Maurischat (RWTH Aachen University, Germany), Ori Parzanchevski (The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel)
abstract: In their seminal paper, Lubotzky, Phillips and Sarnak (LPS) defined the notion of regular Ramanujan graphs and gave a strongly-explicit construction of infinite families of (p+1)-regular Ramanujan Cayley graphs, for infinitely many primes p. In this paper we extend the work of LPS and its successors to bigraphs (biregular bipartite graphs): we investigate the combinatorial properties of various generalizations of the notion of Ramanujan graphs, define a notion of Cayley bigraphs, and give strongly-explicit constructions of infinite families of (p^3+1, p+1)-regular Ramanujan Cayley bigraphs, for infinitely many primes p. In addition, we present a pseudorandomness characterization of Ramanujan bigraphs, and a more general notion of biexpanders. We also show that the graphs we construct exhibit the cutoff phenomenon with bounded window size for the mixing time of non-backtracking random walks, and present some other applications, such as optimal unitary gates in quantum computation.

Abstract—In their seminal paper, Lubotzky, Phillips and Sarnak (LPS) defined the notion of regular Ramanujan graphs and
gave a strongly-explicit construction of infinite families of (p+1)regular Ramanujan Cayley graphs, for infinitely many primes p.
In this paper we extend the work of LPS and its successors
to bigraphs (biregular bipartite graphs): we investigate the
combinatorial properties of various generalizations of the notion
of Ramanujan graphs, define a notion of Cayley bigraphs,
and give strongly-explicit constructions of infinite families of
(p3 + 1, p + 1)-regular Ramanujan Cayley bigraphs, for infinitely
many primes p.
In addition, we present a pseudorandomness characterization
of Ramanujan bigraphs, and a more general notion of biexpanders. We also show that the graphs we construct exhibit the
cutoff phenomenon with bounded window size for the mixing
time of non-backtracking random walks, and present some
other applications, such as optimal unitary gates in quantum
computation.
Index Terms—Expanders, Ramanujan graphs, Cayley bigraphs, Pseudorandomness, Cutoff, Quantum computation

I. I NTRODUCTION
Ramanujan graphs, defined and constructed by Lubotzky,
Phillips and Sarnak (LPS) in [1], are (k + 1)-regular
graphs,
√
whose adjacency eigenvalues satisfy |λ| ≤ 2 k, save for the
“trivial” ones ±(k + 1). The Alon-Boppana theorem [2] tells
us that they are optimal expanders, from the spectral point of
view.
For any distinct odd primes p and q, both congruent to 1
modulo 4, [1] construct p + 1 elements in P GL2 (Fq ) whose
associated Cayley graph is Ramanujan. This construction is
strongly explicit in the sense of [3], [4] – a construction is
called explicit if the entire graph can be computed in polynomial time in its size, and strongly explicit if the neighbors of
every vertex can be computed in polylog time.1

The question of how to define, prove the existence, and
construct non-regular Ramanujan graphs is still, for the most
part, open. In this paper, we give a full treatment of biregular
bipartite graphs, or bigraphs for short. This case is the next
simplest after regular graphs, and has already received attention, for example in the seminal work of Marcus, Spielman
and Srivastava [6]. However, we claim that even the “correct”
definition for a Ramanujan bigraph is not fully settled: we
suggest a stronger definition than that of [6], and show that it
yields several new combinatorial results and applications. We
construct various infinite families of strongly explicit bigraphs
which are Ramanujan (in the strong sense), using a new notion
of “Cayley bigraphs”.

right vertices of degree k + 1, where K > k. The PeronFrobenius

Historically, Greenberg [7] has considered the problem of
defining general Ramanujan graphs and suggested Definition
(1), motivating it by an Alon-Boppana type theorem (see also
[8]). In [9] a stronger Alon-Boppana theorem was proved,
which motivates Definition (2). Further motivation is given
by [10], which shows that random bigraphs are almost adjRamanujan. The strongest Definition (3) goes back to the
classical works of Ihara and Hashimoto on the Riemann
hypothesis for the zeta functions of graphs [11], [12], and
also relates to the results of [13]. Furthermore, [14] shows that
random bigraphs are in fact almost Ramanujan in the strong
sense. Namely, for any ε > 0, a random bigraph has |R| − |L|
√
√
zero eigenvalues, and the others satisfy |λ| − K ≤ k + ε
asymptotically almost surely.
What is known on existence, and on explicit and strongly
explicit constructions? The work of [6] shows that for any K, k
there exist infinite families of Weakly Ramanujan bigraphs –
in fact, they show that every such graph has a two-cover which
is again Weakly Ramanujan, confirming a conjecture of [15].
Their approach was derandomized in [16], [17], yielding an
explicit (but not strongly explicit) polynomial construction. In
[18], [19] a non-explicit construction of Ramanujan bigraphs
(in the strong sense) is given, as quotients of infinite biregular
trees by certain infinite matrix groups. The elements of these
groups are only characterized as the integral solutions of
an explicit set of diophantine equations, so while this is
considered an explicit construction from the point of view
of mathematics, it is far from being explicit in the sense of
computer science as discussed in [3], [4]. We finally mention
that if one allows for families of Ramanujan bigraphs with
unbounded degrees, more constructions exist, e.g. in [20], [21].
Our new construction, which is described in Section II, is
strongly explicit, and yields both adj-Ramanujan and (fully)
Ramanujan families of bigraphs. We give now an example of
one such family which is particularly nice to describe.

We move now to combinatorics. The weak definitions of
Ramanujan bigraphs already yield useful combinatorial properties: adj-Ramanujan bigraphs were used for the construction
of unique-neighbour expanders in [22], and weakly Ramanujan
for the construction of lossless expanders in [23]. Thus, it is
natural to ask what is gained from the strong Ramanujan definition. In Section III we present the following combinatorial
consequences of the strong definition.
1) Cutoff: Ramanujan bigraphs exhibit Diaconis’ cutoff
phenomenon: the total-variation distance of nonbacktracking random walk drops from almost maximal to
almost zero along a period of time which is of order log
log of the size of the graph. Furthermore, for the explicit
graphs that we construct, this period is even bounded.
2) Diameter: The diameter of Ramanujan bigraphs is at
most twice the optimal possible, as given by the Moore
bound (see [24], [25]). Furthermore, almost all pairs of
vertices are within almost optimal distance from one
another.
3) Clash discrepancy: A clash is a pair of edges that
leave different vertices in L and enter the same vertex in R. When counting clashes emanating from two
subsets S, T ⊆ L, Ramanujan bigraphs manifest a
pseudorandom behavior: the discrepancy between the
actual
√ and expected number of clashes is bounded by
2 Kk |S| |T |; We consider this to be the bigraph analogue of the Expander Mixing Lemma.
4) Sparsification of finite geometries: Regular expanders,
and regular Ramanujan graphs in particular, are sparsifiers of the complete graph [26]. It is natural to expect

2092

that Ramanujan bigraphs sparsify complete unbalanced
bipartite graphs, but it turns out that they are actually
sparsifiers of the incidence graphs of lines and hyperplanes in finite geometries.
5) Prime cycle counting: A prime in a graph is a closed
path without backtrackings, which is not a proper power
of one. The zeta function of a graph counts the primes
of each length, and for Ramanujan bigraphs it behaves
as predicted by the (graph analogue of the) Riemann
Hypothesis.
In this note we explain our construction and present the
main applications. The proofs, which often involve deep
excursions into number theory, appear in the preprint [27].
An exception to this are Sections III-A and III-B, where
we go into details regarding pseudorandomness, biexpansion
and sparsification, which may be of interest to the computer
science community.

B. Sparsification
Another perspective on expansion is given by the notion
of spectral sparsification [26]. Roughly speaking, a graph
X is called a sparsifier of a graph Y with the same set
of vertices if αAX − AY is small in an appropriate sense,
where α > 1 is some scaling factor3 . For example, if
X = (L ⊔ R, E) is a k-regular bigraph on 2n vertices and
Y = (L ⊔ R, L × R) is the complete bipartite graph on the
same vertices, then it is easy to see that nk AX − AY ≤ εn
if and only if λ2 (AX ) ≤ εk; thus, sparsification of the
complete regular bigraph is equivalent to being an expander.
However, in the (K + 1, k + 1)-biregular case a Ramanujan
bigraph X = (L ⊔ R, E) is not a good sparsifier for the
complete bipartite graph Y = (L ⊔ R, L × R). The reason
is the excessiveness, namely the kernel of A on the left side:
we require that AX be injective on L, and assuming K > k
the other eigenvalues are bounded away from zero, but for Y
the opposite is true, as the kernel of AY |L is almost maximal:
EY = |L| − 1. This raises the question: what do Ramanujan
bigraphs sparsify? A possible answer is given by line-plane

F. New Ramanujan complexes
Here we explore another application of our work – new
constructions of Ramanujan complexes as Cayley complexes
of finite groups.
Our explicit construction of Ramanujan bigraphs (Section
II) uses the Bruhat-Tits trees associated with projective unitary
groups over the p-adic numbers. For a quadratic imaginary
extension E/Q, the unitary group PU3 (E/Q) embeds in its
p-adic completion, Gp = PU3 (Ep /Qp ). If the prime p remains
prime in the ring of integers of E, then Gp acts on a (p3 +
1, p + 1)-biregular tree, its so called Bruhat-Tits building. Our
Ramanujan bigraphs are obtained by taking quotients of this
tree by carefully chosen lattices in Gp .

simplicial complex. In our constructions, this happens when
